rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The moderate gradient duration provides a useful baseline for subsequent slope and temperature tests.

Lengthen only the gradient to test whether the critical pair responds to reduced slope. The last peak should remain near or below 10 minutes, leaving room to improve resolution without a time penalty.
The critical pair improved with a shallower gradient. Raising phi0 to 0.15 at the same duration further reduces the slope while advancing the last peak, aiming for full resolution within 10 minutes.

Lengthen the gradient by one step to improve the remaining critical pair. Based on the previous slope response and the current 8.62-minute last peak, this should approach full resolution while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.
Injection 4 reached the maximum CRF, so retain it as the benchmark. Raise temperature one step to seek a shorter fully resolved separation and measure the critical pair’s temperature sensitivity.

Test a higher-temperature selectivity regime where the critical pair may separate again after reversing elution order. Shorten the gradient to seek a faster fully resolved method, while retaining injection 4 as the maximum-score benchmark.

Lengthen the gradient one step at 55 C to test whether the new critical pair gains enough resolution. Monitor the pair currently at R = 1.76 as well, since changing slope can improve one separation while worsening another.

The critical pair gains about 0.16 resolution units per added gradient minute, so 18 minutes should bring it above 1.5. The last peak is projected near 9.4 minutes, allowing another maximum-score method if the other pairs remain resolved.

With the maximum CRF secured, test a substantially faster, hotter gradient for a different selectivity regime. The current critical pair may reverse order and regain separation, while the stronger temperature response may preserve the other close pair.

Test one shorter gradient step in the reversed-order regime to see whether the remaining critical pair separates further. Monitor the neighboring pair at R = 1.62, which may limit how much the gradient can be shortened.

Test a higher starting organic fraction to adjust selectivity around the unresolved pair in the fast 60 C method. Restore the eight-minute gradient to protect its neighboring separation, while checking that the early peaks remain retained and resolved.

Lower the starting organic fraction relative to injection 7 to test whether greater initial retention improves the critical middle-pair selectivity. This also protects early-peak resolution and may achieve full resolution faster than the successful 18-minute gradient.

Use the intermediate starting fraction to balance the two critical separations: injections 7 and 12 suggest their resolution limits favor opposite ends of this window. This may fully resolve all peaks with the last peak near eight minutes.
Shorten the fastest fully resolved method by one gradient step. This tests whether the pair at R = 1.77 retains sufficient separation while the other critical pair remains above 1.5.

Lower phi0 one step to improve the unresolved pair, following the selectivity trend between injections 7, 12, and 13. The shorter gradient may keep the other critical pair above 1.5 and deliver full resolution sooner than injection 13.

The maximum score is secured, with injection 15 the fastest fully resolved result. Test the low-temperature selectivity regime with a short gradient to look for a faster separation after temperature-driven elution-order changes.

Test an intermediate temperature with a short gradient to balance the competing middle-pair selectivity trends seen at 45–60 C. Keep the lower starting fraction to protect early retention and assess whether full resolution is possible faster than injection 15.

Test a modestly cooler selectivity regime than the successful 40 C method, using a shorter gradient to target earlier completion. This checks whether cooling can improve the slope-sensitive pair without creating the extensive co-elution seen at 25 C.

Trim the successful injection 15 gradient while preserving its slope exactly. The final peak eluted near organic fraction 0.57, so ending at 0.80 should retain full resolution and the 7.6-minute separation with a shorter programmed gradient.

Use the endpoint grid to test a slope between injections 13 and 14, targeting full resolution with an earlier last peak than injection 13. The 0.75 endpoint remains comfortably above the observed elution window.
Increase the slope slightly from injection 19 to test the speed limit of the fastest fully resolved separation. The pair at R = 1.59 is likely limiting; retain injection 19 if it falls below 1.5.

Back off to the fully resolving slope of injection 19 while trimming the endpoint to 0.65, still above the last peak’s estimated elution fraction of 0.57. This should preserve the maximum CRF with an eight-minute programmed gradient.

Test a compact eight-minute gradient with a slightly shallower slope than injection 20 to increase the limiting pair’s resolution margin. The endpoint remains above the estimated final elution fraction, and the last peak should remain comfortably below 10 minutes.

Refine the fully resolved 55 C method from injection 8 with a slightly steeper slope and a trimmed endpoint. This targets a last peak near nine minutes while retaining more resolution margin than the fastest method, injection 22.

Test a slightly steeper slope than injection 20 to approach the full-resolution boundary, targeting a last peak near 7.6 minutes. Retain injection 22 as the fastest demonstrated maximum-score method if the critical pair drops below 1.5.
